english-1.title: Passage I
english-1.html:
Missouri’s Elephants

My sister Marina looked at me expectantly while I eyed the boulders at Missouri’s Elephant Rocks State Park. They didn’t really look like elephants—maybe more like giant baked potatoes [1]spread on a baking sheet. I told her as much, and she rolled her eyes, saying that the name conveys less about shape than it does about size. The boulders were colossal; some rivaled the size of elephants. [2]Some like, the 680-ton favorite “Dumbo,” were even bigger. Marina, [3]who had studied the rocks in her graduate program, talked as we made our way through the park. She clearly had the geology of the park memorized.

About 1.5 billion years ago, volcanic calderas [4]covered a section of Missouri in what is now southeastern Missouri. These calderas formed as a result of molten rock (magma) and gas squeezing up through underlying chambers and causing a buildup of pressure just beneath the surface rock. When enough pressure mounted, most of the magma blasted through the rock, carving out miles-wide craters. In the aftermath, the small amounts of magma left behind in the chambers began cooling into granite rock. [5]When shards of surface rock and volcanic ash tumbled into the newly exposed chambers, covering the cooling magma with a layer thousands of feet thick.

Marina pointed toward the line of pink granite boulders on the hill in front of us. She explained that, as the years [6]passed, the overlying layer of rock would of eroded to reveal the granite. Wind and water rounded the jagged edges of the blocks and polished [7]this into these boulders. In time, the constant cycle of uplift and erosion would expose more underlying granite blocks— [8] another generation of elephants.

I pressed my palms against one of the elephants, trying to imagine the incredible heat that forged the stone. Marina began climbing, using the [9]crevices in the rock to hoist herself up. She reached the top, about twenty feet above me, before she looked down and grinned. I grinned back, [10]marveling at how well my sister and I were getting along here at Elephant Rocks State Park.

english-2.title: Passage Ii
english-2.html:
The Surprising Allure of Slow TV

In 2009, Norway’s public broadcasting station, NRK, unexpectedly [11]launched: a new national pastime, slow TV. NRK producers aired the seven-hour, fourteen-minute “Bergensbanen Minute by Minute.” It showed continuous footage of the 309-mile Bergensbanen train route from Oslo, the capital, to Bergen, a city on Norway’s west coast.

Expecting only about 2,000 viewers, the producers were shocked when 1.2 million Norwegians tuned in. Both the station and social media [12]was flooded with suggestions for the next project.

[13]In 2011, NRK took on an extremely ambitious project—a five-and-a-half-day boat cruise along Norway’s most famous shipping route. The Hurtigruten voyage was broadcast live, and Norwegians did more than watch. Some crowded the ports along the route; [14]some were seen standing all alone on rocky outcroppings; others actually sailed alongside the ship. In addition to stunning landscapes, sunsets, and coastal architecture, the footage captured thousands of people enthusiastically waving to compatriots watching from home. The television audience included more than three-fifths of the country’s five million people, an [15]all-time high for NRK.

english-3.title: Passage Iii
english-3.html:
Goode’s Idea

[16] On July 14, 1885, Sarah E. Goode, a furniture store owner on Chicago’s South Side, received a US patent—one of the first granted to an African American woman—for her folding cabinet bed. Unlike the more modern Murphy bed, which is stored vertically against a wall and camouflaged as a cabinet, Goode’s bed hid inside a free-standing cabinet that also functioned as a desk. Meant to meet the needs of city-dwelling customers, [17]people whom needed furniture that maximized small apartment spaces, Goode’s bed entered the market as the first space-saving design of its kind.

Having exposure to carpentry (both her father and husband had careers as carpenters), Goode used innovative design to simplify the desk-to-bed conversion. Essentially, the piece consisted of three tiers. At the bottom was the base, the width of [18]the base dictated the width of the unfolded bed. A cabinet on top of the base housed a [19]mattress folded into thirds, and on top of the cabinet were the writing surface and storage cubbies that made the piece a functioning desk.

To turn the desk into a bed, one had to first lift the desk’s writing surface, which was connected to the back of the piece with hinges, and push it up and back until it stood upright, perpendicular to the floor. [20]For example, the now-vertical writing surface [21]could serve as the bed’s headboard.

Attached to the base with hinges, the front and back walls of the cabinet could be pushed down to create a platform the length of a standard-size bed. After securing the platform—Goode’s patent describes the series of braces and springs used for structural support—one unfolded the full-length mattress. The bed [22]conversion from desk to bed was complete.

[23]Born of necessity, the invention appealed to nineteenth-century customers. People visited Goode’s store to purchase the well-crafted piece, causing a boost in overall store profits. [24]Random, I know, but over one hundred years later, Goode’s influence endures in the innovative, multifunctional furniture typical of contemporary design.

english-4.title: Passage Iv
english-4.html:
Drumming Up a World of Sound

In the 1980s, Evelyn Glennie attended London’s Royal Academy of Music. [26]In retrospect, her professors cautioned her that no one had succeeded—[27]nor could succeed—as a full-time solo percussionist. Unwilling to accept this advice, Glennie proceeded to put solo percussion on the map. Little had been written for the genre, so Glennie composed or commissioned hundreds of pieces, [28]captivating audiences with her innovative musicianship. She also earned acclaim through an array of collaborations with groups ranging from symphonies to rock bands.

Whether in a classroom or a concert hall, Glennie always performs barefoot. Having lost nearly all hearing ability as a child, she realized at the age of twelve—when she began studying percussion—that she could listen with more than her ears. Having bare feet helps her feel vibrations [29]and detect certain pitches by using her feet to perceive the vibrations.

Feeling sound throughout her body has given Glennie insight as a composer. She listens [30]quite intensely to the clatter of a city street as she does to the harmonies of an orchestra, internalizing experiences that enrich her understanding of sound.

english-5.title: Passage V
english-5.html:
Nature’s Bug Spray

[1] In Scandinavian folklore, the marsh Labrador tea plant, a flowering shrub that grows abundantly in northern regions, [31]have been esteemed as a convenient and natural moth repellant. Since the medieval era, people have stored the shrub’s evergreen branches with winter clothing in an effort to deter [32]wool-gnawing moths. The [33]practice of storing the branches with winter clothing remains popular today. However, reasons for its success have been largely speculative—that is, until recently, when scientists inadvertently uncovered an explanation.

[2] In 2009, a team of ecologists, led by Professor Jarmo Holopainen, traipsed through a forest in Finland to identify gaseous emissions of tree and plant foliage. [A] While [34]noting mountain birch tree emissions, Holopainen noticed ledene, ledol, and palustrol—chemical compounds uncharacteristic of birch trees. [B] Typically, these compounds are emitted by marsh Labrador tea plants, several [35]of them grew near the birch.

[3] [C] Holopainen [36]theorized that: when the neighboring marsh teas emitted their gaseous bouquets, the birch leaves absorbed and rereleased these compounds. [D] He knew that plants emitting ledene, ledol, and palustrol did so for self-preservation following an herbivore attack. In other words, the release of these compounds served as a bug repellant, warding off further attacks. The birch tree, then, [37]was engaging in what is termed “associational resistance” with marsh teas, absorbing and releasing compounds that deter herbivores.

[4] The findings not only substantiated long-held folk beliefs about this natural moth repellant but also clarified how ecosystems balance plant and herbivore fitness. This particular case demonstrated that different plant species growing in close proximity depend on one another for survival. [38]Still, Holopainen’s study highlighted the importance of considering ecological effects from the perspective of plants within a community rather than as individuals.

english-6.title: Passage Vi
english-6.html:
AI-Assisted Judging: A Gold Medal Idea

[1] The athletic feats performed at the Olympics never cease to amaze me. A snowboarder corkscrews through the sky. A leaping figure skater lands perfectly on one foot. Two divers simultaneously spring from their parallel boards. As a casual [41]enthusiast, I often struggle to distinguish the great performances, from the merely good. For Olympic judges, though, the slight differences matter—a lot. [A] Unfortunately, even these experts can miss [42]an error separating a performance earning a nine point five from a coveted ten. Thus, [43]to ensure Olympic athletes are judged fairly, we should start incorporating artificial intelligence (AI) into the process used to evaluate athletes’ performances.

[2] So how do artificially intelligent judges work? First, an AI model is trained on countless hours of [44]footage, effectively teaching it to identify tricks, distinguish between a good landing and an okay landing, and see small flaws, such as the slight under rotation of a spin. Then, during a competition, a handful of high-definition cameras record an athlete and construct a three-dimensional image of their body. [B] The image is then fed into the trained AI model, which precisely analyzes each angle and movement beyond the capabilities of a human.

[3] [45]Some might argue that AI will soon replace human judges altogether, but this is not the case. Elements like artistry and style (what make these subjective sports so special) are nearly impossible for AI to evaluate, [46]thus, it’s vital that we keep humans at the center of judging these sports. [C] However, even at their best, humans can miss things or grow fatigued at the end of a long day. [47]Complimenting human judges with this would allow them to review [48]complex routines and tricks or help them more fairly resolve a challenge from an athlete.

[4] AI-assisted review is already effectively being used in sports like tennis to determine line calls, and it’s being tested by Major League Baseball to help call balls and strikes. [D] If we can make judging Olympic sports fairer by using AI in a supportive role, [49]we should look to employ the newest technology.

reading-1.title: Passage I
reading-1.html:
Passage I

LITERARY NARRATIVE: Passage A is adapted from “Among Saudi Sands” by Keija Parssinen (©2012 by Keija Parssinen).

Passage B is from “Winding Threads” by Kate Maloy (©2008 by

Kate Maloy).

Passage A by Keija Parssinen

I learned how to leave home from a young age—
how to pack a suitcase, how to do a final scan of the
small room I shared with my brother. The rituals of
departure came easily to me; I was an expatriate child.
Where I was from and where I called home were not
the same place.
I remember the European vacations that served as
stepping stones in my family’s yearly journey across
the ocean from Saudi Arabia, where we lived, to
Southern California, where my grandparents lived, and
where my parents were technically from. Though first
you’d have to trace them back through the valleys of
Lebanon and the bustle of Tunisian souqs and the
wadis of Jordan, and of course, through the salt-ridden
Gulf town where they had settled their family.
On the interminable flights to the States, we
children made nests of thin airplane blankets on the
floor where we were supposed to put our feet, but
where instead we put ourselves, tucked away like
carry-on luggage.
The rhythms of that multi-legged trip, which
spanned three continents, reverberated in me so that I
came to define my year by that annual departure, when
our family left on ‘repat’—short for repatriation. And
of course, there was always the return trip to the desert
peninsula that had been my home since birth, which I
and my siblings loved, but which my parents met with
dread, passing the in-flight hours on the KLM flight by
recounting events of the previous six weeks—the
bottles of Italian wine imbibed beneath fragrant grape
arbors, the walks in the foothills of the Alps, the
electric-blue swimming pools and churning coastline of
California.
But I longed for the blast of humid air against my
face when I descended the plane in Dhahran. To me,
the pleasures of vacation never outweighed those of
home, perhaps because I had a child’s limited appetite,
or perhaps the desert had worked its way inside me—
its dust and oil-flare air coating my lungs, giving me
both asthma and the feeling that I belonged to the
place.
There was one voyage out, though, that did not
involve return. In July 1992, Dad took early retirement.
In a photo from that time, I’m looking out across the
water, my face twisted up with the realization that
these are the days of ‘lasts’—last time swimming in the
Arabian Gulf, last time racing up the giant dune at the
end of the beach.

Passage B by Kate Maloy

Several years ago, I tallied up all the states, towns,
and dwellings in which I had ever lived and found that
I’d moved thirty-five times in my life. Now the number
is thirty-seven, and I’ve finally stopped thinking that I
won’t ever move again.
The last time I thought that was eight years ago,
when I left Pennsylvania for Vermont with my third
husband. (Clearly, I have covered more than
geographic ground.) We weathered five winters in
northern New England, the last of which proved
especially bitter and far too hard on my husband’s
joints. So we headed west, and now, after a year on
hold in a place we didn’t like, we’ve settled into a
small house on the Oregon coast, where there are no
extremes of cold or heat, and you don’t have to shovel
rain. I won’t change husbands again, but I have a
feeling that this is not my last house.
I never meant to be so peripatetic. What a good
word—peripatetic. It’s related to peripeteia, which, in
the stage world (and all the world’s a stage), is linked
inseparably with anagnorisis. Peripeteia is a sudden
reversal, an unforeseen event or crisis. Anagnorisis is a
revelation, discovery, or lesson. Each can lead to the
other, and back again.
My relocations have almost always involved this
back-and-forth between reversal and revelation.
Sometimes, moving itself has been the reversal, a
deliberate choice, but one that has bred crisis or
surprise in its unfolding. In my twenties and early
thirties, I made this choice often, moving from here to
there because the grass looked greener or the job more
interesting or the guy more enticing. Naturally,
wherever I went, there I was, with reality to face and
lessons to learn. When things did not turn out as I
expected (nearly always), I had to figure out how to
deal with the jolts and tremors.
In childhood, of course, the decision to move was
never mine. My father’s company would hand it down,
and off we would go again, to another branch in
another part of the country. Good-bye to friends and
houses, hello to new schools and kids and teachers,
hello to trembling knees and knots in my stomach until
I learned the way to my classrooms, until some of the
new kids became friends. Then, after a few years,
good-bye again.

reading-2.title: Passage Ii
reading-2.html:
Passage II

INFORMATIONAL: This passage is from the essay “Great Zimbabwe (Eleventh–Fifteenth Centuries)” by the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

The ruins of this complex of massive stone walls
undulate across almost 1,800 acres of present-day
southeastern Zimbabwe. Begun during the eleventh
century A.D. by Bantu-speaking ancestors of the
Shona, Great Zimbabwe was constructed and expanded
for more than 300 years in a local style that eschewed
rectilinearity for flowing curves. Neither the first nor
the last of some 300 similar complexes located on the
Zimbabwean plateau, Great Zimbabwe is set apart by
the terrific scale of its structure. Its most formidable
edifice has walls as high as 36 feet extending
approximately 820 feet, making it the largest ancient
structure south of the Sahara Desert. In the 1800s,
European travelers and English colonizers attributed
the architecture to foreign powers. Such attributions
were dismissed when archaeological investigations
conducted during the first decades of the twentieth
century confirmed both the antiquity of the site and its
African origins.
Great Zimbabwe’s most enduring and impressive
remains are its stone walls. These walls were
constructed from granite blocks gathered from the
exposed rock of the surrounding hills. Since this rock
naturally splits into even slabs and can be broken into
portable sizes, it provided a convenient and readily
available building resource. All of Great Zimbabwe’s
walls were fitted without the use of mortar by laying
stones one on top of the other, each layer slightly more
recessed than the last to produce a stabilizing inward
slope. Early examples were coarsely fitted using rough
blocks and incorporated features of the landscape such
as boulders into the walls. Over the years the technique
was refined, and later walls were fitted together closely
and evenly over long, serpentine courses to produce
remarkably finished surfaces.
Little is known about the Bantu-speaking people
who built Great Zimbabwe or how their society was
organized. The ruling elite appears to have controlled
wealth through the management of cattle. At its height,
Great Zimbabwe is estimated to have had a population
greater than 10,000, although the majority lived at
some distance from the large stone buildings. Only
200 to 300 members of the elite classes are thought to
have lived within Great Zimbabwe’s massive edifices.
The enormous walls are the best-preserved
testaments of Great Zimbabwe’s past and the largest
example of an architectural type seen in archaeological
sites throughout the region. The function of these stone
walls, however, has often been misinterpreted. At first
glance, these massive nonsupportive walls appear
purely defensive. But scholars doubt they ever served a
martial purpose and have argued instead that cattle and
people were valued above land. The walls are thought
to have been a symbolic show of authority, designed to
preserve the privacy of royal families and set them
apart from and above commoners. It is also important
to note that the walls surrounded and later adjoined
huts made of daga (mud and thatch), linked with them
to form a series of courtyards. Since Great Zimbabwe’s
daga elements have long since eroded, the remaining
stone walls provide only partial evidence of the
architecture’s original appearance.
In addition to architecture, Great Zimbabwe’s
most famous works of art are the eight birds carved of
soapstone that were found in its ruins. The birds
surmount columns more than a yard tall and are
themselves on average sixteen inches tall. The
sculptures combine both human and avian elements,
substituting human features like lips for a beak and
five-toed feet for claws. Scholars have suggested that
the birds served as emblems of royal authority, perhaps
representing the ancestors of Great Zimbabwe’s rulers.
Although their precise significance is still unknown,
these sculptures remain powerful symbols of rule in the
modern era, adorning the flag of Zimbabwe as national
emblems.

reading-3.title: Passage Iii
reading-3.html:
Passage III

INFORMATIONAL: This passage is adapted from the essay “The Sea of Information” by Andrea Barrett (©2004 by Andrea Barrett).

There are excellent novels that do make
arguments, and are as essentially polemical as a work
of nonfiction: Dickens’s Hard Times comes to mind.
But these aren’t the novels, for whatever reasons, that I
most love; nor are they what I attempt to write. Usually
what I’m trying to build isn’t an argument, isn’t overtly
didactic, doesn’t state its premises clearly, often
doesn’t operate linearly, and can’t be reduced to a clear
statement.
It took being in the company of a group of
scholars to teach me that when I do what, up until then,
I had always thought of as “research,” I was only
skimming the surface. I know a little about a lot of
things, but the only thing I really know well is
storytelling, in all its forms—and that’s the end my
so-called research serves. Although most of my fiction
is set in the past and employs the materials of history,
I’m not trying to discover new facts, or to develop new
hypotheses, or in some sense prove “how it was.” I’m
trying to shape a narrative that allows a reader to feel
what it was like to be a particular person, or set of
persons, caught in a particular situation at a particular
place and time. When I looked at the sugar factory in
Williamsburg and dug up early photographs of it or
articles about how sugar was processed there, I was
looking for those details that would allow me to
imagine one person working in and moving through
that space; I was imagining it as background. A social
historian, looking at the same material, might ask what
wages were, what the ethnicity of the workers was,
where those workers lived, who got paid what for what
hours. Facts, from which inferences could be drawn. I
was looking for something else.
I wanted what would help me not to tell, but to
show. If I could convey what I wanted to convey by a
set of logically ordered and clear statements, I’d do
that. But a good novel or story or poem tries to convey
a different kind of knowledge, and to operate on the
reader in a different way, through the emotions and the
senses. Facts can help evoke emotion, especially those
that transmit texture, tonality, and sensual detail. But
facts can’t drive a piece. Research, no matter how
compelling, may give me the bones of a fiction but
never the breath and the blood. It’s a wonderful,
sometimes immensely useful tool that helps give me
something to write about. But without the transforming
force of the imagination, the result is only information.
In 1936, Walter Benjamin wrote this:
Every morning brings us the news of the globe,
and yet we are poor in noteworthy stories. This
is because no event any longer comes to us
without already being shot through with
explanation. In other words, by now almost
nothing that happens benefits storytelling;
almost everything benefits information.
Actually, it is half the art of storytelling to
keep a story free from explanation as one
reproduces it. [. . .] The value of information
does not survive the moment in which it was
new. It lives only at that moment; it has to
surrender to it completely and explain itself to
it without losing any time.
Information, information. I was drowning in it,
one stream pouring in from the daily news of the world,
the other bubbling up from the library stacks, while all
around me people used it to build explanations for the
present and the past. Every day I’d learn something
more about the world. And every day I felt farther
away from the writing itself. It was as if, to hark back
again to Hard Times, I had turned while my attention
had drifted into the student in Professor Gradgrind’s
class who, when asked to define a horse, responded:
“Quadruped. Graminivorous. Forty teeth,
namely twenty-four grinders, four eye-teeth,
and twelve incisive. Sheds coat in the spring;
in marshy countries, sheds hoofs, too. Hoofs
hard, but requiring to be shod with iron. Age
known by marks in the mouth.”
Caught up in learning about the equivalent of
grinders and eyeteeth, I’d forgotten that while facts
may be in a text—sometimes delectably—they can’t be
the text itself. Slowly I began to relearn something I’d
once grasped, but had lost sight of: that emotion—that
central element of fiction—derives not from
information or explanation, nor from a logical
arrangement of facts, but specifically from powerful
images and from the qualities of language: diction,
rhythm, form, structure, association, metaphor. And
sometimes I also had glimmers of another thing I’d
once known: how effectively information can be used
to wall off emotion.

reading-4.title: Passage Iv
reading-4.html:
Passage IV

INFORMATIONAL: This passage is adapted from the article “All Men Can’t Jump” by David Stipp (©2012 by The Slate Group LLC). This graphic is adapted from the article “Endurance Running and the Evolution of Homo” by Dennis M. Bramble and Daniel E. Lieberman (©2004 by Macmillan Magazines Ltd.).

Humans are the right honorable kings and queens
of the planet when it comes to long-distance running.
The Wales Man vs. Horse Marathon has helped
demonstrate that. Its originator was a Welsh pub owner
named Gordon Green. One day in 1979 he got into an
argument with an equestrian friend about the relative
strengths of men and horses as distance runners. Green
insisted a human could beat a horse in a long race, and
to prove his point he helped instigate the marathon in
1980. For the next 24 years, he found himself losing
the argument as riders on horseback left human runners
behind. But then it finally happened—in 2004 a British
man named Huw Lobb won. Three years later
Germany’s Florian Holzinger outran the horses, as did
one other human contestant. The media loved it—a
predictable farce had become a man-bites-dog story.
Bookies were less enthused; they had to pay out on bets
made at 16-to-1 odds favoring the horses.
The oddsmakers would have known better if
they’d been following the work of Harvard
anthropologist Daniel Lieberman and University of
Utah biologist Dennis Bramble. They jointly proposed
in a 2004 paper that we’re superlatively endowed by
evolution to go long. As a species, our long-striding
legs are packed with springlike tendons, muscles, and
ligaments that enable us to briefly store elastic energy
as we come down on a foot and then recoil to help
propel us forward. Tellingly, the most important of
these springs, our big, strong Achilles tendons, aren’t
found in early human precursors such as
Australopithecus—it seems that the high-end tendons
evolved along with other adaptations for distance
running in the genus Homo when it appeared on the
African savannah about 2 million years ago.
We’ve inherited large leg and foot joints from
those ancestors, which spread out high forces that must
be absorbed when running. To help ensure stability on
two legs, we have big gluteus maximus muscles.
(Chimps, which are incapable of distance running, have
comparatively tiny butts.) Our clever torsos are
designed to “counter-rotate” versus the hips as we run,
also aiding stability. And we have an unusually large
percentage of fatigue-resistant, slow-twitch muscle
fibers, which make for endurance rather than speed. By
contrast, most animals are geared for sprinting because
they’re either predators that chase or prey that run
away, and their muscles thus have much higher
percentages of fast-twitch fibers than ours. (Cheetahs’
hind-leg muscles are the fast-twitch-richest of all.)
But what most sets us apart as runners is that
we’re really cool—we naked apes are champion
sweaters and can dissipate body heat faster than any
other large mammal. Our main rivals for the
endurance-running crown fall into two groups:
migratory ungulates, such as horses and wildebeest,
and social carnivores, such as dogs and hyenas. They
can easily out-sprint us by galloping. But none can
gallop very far without overheating—they largely rely
on panting to keep cool, and they can’t pant when
galloping, for panting involves taking very rapid,
shallow breaths that would interfere with respiration
when running. Dogs can gallop for only about 10 to
15 minutes before reverting to a trot, and so their
distance-running speed tops out at about 3.8 meters per
second. Horses’ average distance-running speed is
5.8 meters per second—a canter. Wildebeests’ is
5.1 meters per second.
Elite human runners, however, can sustain speeds
up to 6.5 meters per second. Even run-of-the-mill
joggers typically do between 3.2 and 4.2 meters per
second, which means they can outrun dogs at distances
greater than two kilometers.
Our “sustainable distance” is also hard to beat.
African hunting dogs typically travel an average of
10 kilometers a day. Wolves and hyenas tend to go
about 14 and 19 kilometers, respectively. In repeated
distance runs, horses can cover about 20 kilometers a
day. Vast throngs of human runners, by comparison,
routinely run 42.2-kilometer marathons in just a few
hours, and each year tens of thousands of people
complete ultra-marathons of 100 kilometers and longer.

science-2.title: Passage Ii
science-2.html:
Passage II

When the ozone (O3) in air is mixed with an acidic solution of iodide ion (I−), the O3 reacts to form triiodide ion (I3−), O2, and H2O.

O3 + 3I− + 2H+ → I3− + O2 + H2O

Students performed an experiment to determine the concentration of O3 in samples of air. Figure 1 shows the relationship between the concentration of I3−, in μmol/L, and the concentration of O3, in parts per billion (ppb), under the conditions of the experiment.

Experiment

At each of 4 outdoor sites, the students assembled the apparatus shown in Figure 2. First, they attached a long piece of tubing to a stand so that one end of the tubing was 1.5 m above the ground. Then, they placed the other end of the tubing into one hole of a 2-holed stopper. Next, they placed one end of a shorter piece of tubing into the second hole of the 2-holed stopper and attached the other end of the shorter tubing to a vacuum pump.

At each site, the students performed the following 2 steps every half hour from 12:30 p.m. to 5:30 p.m. on a particular day:

1. A 10.0 mL volume of an aqueous acidic solution having a 10 mg/mL concentration of I− was placed into a clean, empty test tube that was then sealed with the 2-holed stopper.

2. The vacuum pump was turned on for 25 min to collect an air sample. Then, the pump was turned off and the concentration of I3−, in micromoles/liter (μmol/L), in the solution was measured.

The results are shown in Figure 3.

Figures adapted from J. V. Seeley et al., “A Simple Method for Measuring Ground-Level Ozone in the Atmosphere.” ©2005 by the Division of Chemical Education, Inc., American Chemical Society.

science-4.html:
Passage IV

A planetary transit occurs when a planet passes between Earth and the Sun. For a study, student groups in 6 locations worldwide observed the times at which Venus moved into specific reference positions during its June 2004 transit. Figure 1 shows 4 reference positions (first, second, third, and fourth contacts) along the transit path.

Study

At each viewing location, the transit was observed using telescopes with solar filters, which only allow the transmission of light with a wavelength of 656 nanometers (nm). Students at each location used a clock calibrated to Coordinated Universal Time (referred to as UTC), the time at Earth’s 0° longitude, to record the time at which Venus was observed in the second and third contact positions. The ability to view the full transit required that the Sun be above the horizon during the entire transit and that the local weather not interfere with a clear view of the Sun. science-5.title: Passage V
science-5.html:
Passage V

An air bubble in liquid accelerates upward due to a buoyant force. If the bubble is in contact with a solid surface, a friction force proportional to its velocity will oppose the motion. When these 2 effects are balanced, the bubble moves at a constant speed: the terminal velocity. Scientists performed 3 studies to examine the effects of bubble radius, surface angle, and liquid composition on the terminal velocity.

An apparatus (see Figure 1) was constructed from a glass cylinder (GC) that was sealed at one end and printed with a scale in millimeters. The GC was clamped to an adjustable platform and capped. A syringe was attached to the platform, and the needle was inserted through the GC’s cap. A laser pointer parallel to the GC was pointed at a vertical ruler. A video camera was placed above the GC.

Study 1

The GC was filled with H2O, and Steps 1−5 were performed.

1. The platform was set at an angle, θ, having 1 of 7 values.

2. A bubble was released from the syringe into the GC.

3. Video of the bubble was recorded.

4. The bubble’s radius and terminal velocity were determined.

5. Steps 2−4 were repeated for 6 more bubbles, each having a different radius.

These procedures were then repeated at the other 6 angles (see Figure 2).

Study 2

The procedures of Study 1 were repeated, except the GC was filled with 10 millimolar (mM) KCl solution (see Figure 3).

Study 3

The procedures of Study 1 were repeated, except the GC was filled with 100 mM KCl solution (see Figure 4).

Figures adapted from the article “Effect of Disjoining Pressure on Terminal Velocity of a Bubble Sliding Along an Inclined Wall” by L.A. Del Castillo et al. (©2011 by Elsevier).

science-6.title: Passage Vi
science-6.html:
Passage VI

Nuclear fusion is the process by which 2 nuclei combine to form a single, more massive nucleus. In this process, 1 or more subatomic particles (such as a proton, p, or a neutron, n) may also be produced. A teacher asked her students to consider the following 2 nuclear reactions.

Reaction 1: H12 + H12 → He24

Reaction 2: H12 + H13 → He24 + n01

Each reactant and product has 2 numbers associated with it: a mass number (the number on top) and an atomic number (the number on the bottom). Further, the atomic number indicates the positive charge. The teacher then asked the students to determine which of the reactions, if either, can occur.

Student 1

For a fusion reaction to occur, mass number and atomic number must both be conserved. (A conserved quantity is one whose value does not change during a reaction.) In both Reaction 1 and Reaction 2, the sum of the mass numbers of the reactants is equal to the sum of the mass numbers of the products. Similarly, the sum of the atomic numbers of the reactants is equal to the sum of the atomic numbers of the products. Thus, mass number and atomic number are both conserved in both reactions, so both reactions can occur.

Student 2

Student 1 is correct; however, in addition, if each reactant is positively charged, each product must also be positively charged. The product of Reaction 1 is positively charged, but the products of Reaction 2 include a neutral particle. Thus, Reaction 1 can occur, but Reaction 2 cannot.

Student 3

For a fusion reaction to occur, mass number and electric charge must both be conserved, and there must be at least 2 products. Though mass number and electric charge are both conserved in both reactions, Reaction 1 has only 1 product. Thus, Reaction 2 can occur, but Reaction 1 cannot.

Student 4

For a fusion reaction to occur, electric charge must be conserved, there must be at least 2 products, and if each reactant is positively charged, each product must also be positively charged. Thus, neither Reaction 1 nor Reaction 2 can occur.

Following the students’ responses, the teacher provided them with 2 example reactions (Reactions Y and Z) that can both occur.

Reaction Y: He23 + He23 → He24 + p11 + p11

Reaction Z: H12 + H12 → He23 + n01

science-7.title: Passage Vii
science-7.html:
Passage VII

Gibberulus gibberulus, a marine snail, jumps to escape predation from Conus marmoreus, another marine snail. A study was done to investigate the effect of CO2 concentrations in seawater on this escape behavior.

Study

Eighty G. gibberulus were equally divided into 2 groups (Groups 1 and 2), and 80 C. marmoreus were equally divided into 2 groups (Groups 3 and 4). Groups 1 and 3 were stored in separate tanks containing seawater with an ambient ocean CO2 concentration (a concentration equal to that typically found in the ocean). Groups 2 and 4 were stored in the same manner except that the tanks contained seawater with an elevated ocean CO2 concentration (2.5 times the ambient ocean CO2 concentration).

For each snail in Groups 1 and 3, the following steps were done:

1. A thin, transparent barrier was placed in the center of a new tank containing seawater with an ambient ocean CO2 concentration.

2. A single G. gibberulus and a single C. marmoreus were each removed from their storage tanks and placed 10 mm from either side of the barrier, facing each other.

3. Snails were observed for 5 min, and the following values were determined: the time, t, between when observations began and the G. gibberulus’s first jump; the number of jumps, NJ, by the G. gibberulus; and the distance, d, between the G. gibberulus and the C. marmoreus at 5 min.

Steps 1−3 were repeated for each snail in Groups 2 and 4 except that the tank contained seawater with an elevated ocean CO2 concentration. Table 1 shows, for each pair of groups studied, the total number of G. gibberulus that jumped at least once (NS) and the average values of t, NJ, and d.
